findings.text: The first paragraph says plainly what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. A newcomer can say what it is after reading three sentences.
findings.source: header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository."

findings.text: A jump link near the top takes the reader straight to the next steps, so they do not have to scroll past the long study to find what to do.
findings.source: header lede: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete: what you need first, how to clone and run setup, and a first command to try. A newcomer can act on them.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page is Athena's site, but its title and almost all of its content are about another project, firstmate. A newcomer may at first think they have landed on the wrong site.
findings.source: title: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The page promises request-to-commit with costs and verdicts, but its example is a study of another project. Nothing shows a request, its commit, the costs or the verdict, so the link between the demo and the main promise is left for the reader to work out.
findings.source: header lede: "It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable." vs. "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project"

findings.text: This link speaks to the site owner, not a visitor. A newcomer has no proposals, so the link is confusing.
findings.source: header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The firstmate sections are dense and full of terms and internal ids (t1, c31, mode=retain). A first-time visitor will likely skim them. The early word list and the Glossary help, but the page is long for its purpose.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: The page is open about what it does not know. Several glossary entries say the term is undefined in the source. This builds trust in the claim tracing but leaves some terms unclear.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a captain call."

findings.text: The page says clearly that firstmate was never run, only read. That supports the page's promise of accountability.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read"

findings.text: Every claim links to exact lines in firstmate at the pinned commit. This shows the traceability Athena promises in a way a newcomer can check.
findings.source: Claims and sources: links such as "bin/fm-spawn.sh:194-197" at the pinned commit

findings.text: Cost is part of the pitch, but neither Next steps nor anywhere else says what running Athena costs or what account it needs beyond Claude Code.
findings.source: header lede: "and records what each step cost"
